About this citation

Several letters quote an earlier author — Cleanthes, Hecato, Epicurus — and in those the quoted sentence is that author's, delivered in Seneca's Latin. The archive records the inner attribution in the source field where it is known.

#### About Seneca

Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE–65 CE) was a Cordoban-born Stoic, tragic playwright, and adviser—later forced suicide victim—under Nero.

### Interpretation

Seneca is using death as a description rather than a threat. His claim is that a person is constituted by what they attend to, so time emptied of anything demanding is not rest but the suspension of the self. He is writing to a friend considering retirement, and the point is that withdrawal without study does not produce freedom, only vacancy. Leisure in his account is not idleness but the condition for the work that matters.

#### Why it matters

It distinguishes rest from vacancy. Time off restores when there is something to return to; without it, the same hours do not recover anything.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Leisure without study is death — a tomb…”?

“Leisure without study is death — a tomb…” comes from Letters to Lucilius, Ep. 82.3 (c. 62–65 CE), attributed to Seneca.

#### What does Seneca mean by learning?

Education is not only information transfer; it is the shaping of attention and character. Confucian learning, Socratic midwifery, and Deweyan growth offer rival models. This passage enters that discussion through learning, life.
